title: Non-trad just trying to find his way...
content:
Hello! I'm a non-trad, just weighing a bunch of different options. Currently, I'm interested in gen surg and EM, but I'm trying to really give other specialties a shot - especially given that I have a kid on the way and I don't want medicine to be my entire identity.

I think the bottom line for me is that if I were to go into FM, I don't think I'd be happy or stimulated doing outpatient clinic and trying to churn through 20+ patients a day. Is it possible to practice rural medicine as a "weekend warrior" while still practicing medicine in a metro area? My wife won't let me live out in the boonies, but rural medicine in itself sounds pretty cool, and providing care where it's disappearing is pretty important. 

  
Alternatively, how difficult is it to set up and maintain DPC? It sounds very attractive to me, and I feel it would give me the $$$ and autonomy to do other meaningful things, such as getting a medical van and providing care in rural areas.

I'm prior military and have worked in the ED, so EM and gen surg are what I naturally gravitate towards, but the thought of DPC (and not doing gen surg) also sounds great.

title: Best place to hire a doc to join my DPC practice in Missoula, MT?
content:
Howdy! I run a 2 provider DPC practice with my partner (both MDs, partner is functional medicine trained as well) in Missoula, MT that we opened last fall and have already outgrown our space (currently doubling the clinic from 6 to 12 exam rooms) and almost filled our panels! We need to hire a doc sometime in the next few months, and I have no idea where to start that search. We've got a few other docs in the pipeline that we're planning to hire over the next few years as they finish their PSLF requirements, but we need someone before that! I'm not sure if it's kosher to post this kind of thing here, but figured I'd give it a shot.

Currently we work 4.5 days per week, 6 patients per day (hour long visits only), but anticipate going to a 3.5 or maybe even 3 day work week with 8 patients per day as we expand. \~500 patient panel is full but general comp will eventually be based on 75% of revenue generated after overhead, anticipated salary of $300k+. We can start with that model if desired or salary at $220k for 2 years then move to eat what you kill. Partner option available with negotiable buy-in after 2 year employee agreement. We compensate our MA's fantastically, have a business manager, and have a gorgeous custom built clinic space with 20 foot ceilings on top of a hill with panoramic views. It's truly the best possible place to work! Where does one even post a job opening like this?!

Thanks so much!

title: FM vs Peds for taking care of kids
content:
Hello so I'm a third year med student that is constantly going back and forth between FM->sports medicine and med/peds-> sports medicine. I know that FM has better infrastructure for pursuing sports compared to any other specialty that can match into it which is a pro, and in addition to that it's one year shorter and wayyy easier to match which is also an enormous pro. 

The thing is that while outpatient sounds great to me on paper (have the goal of having my own dpc practice in the future), I reallyyyy like doing inpatient and also enjoyed my inpatient peds rotation. 

I would like to be very comfortable with seeing kids, and when I see posts on here about FM doctors not having their spouses or family members trust them with their professional opinions about kids and going out of their way to consult a pediatrician it's definitely discouraging. In addition to this I know a lot of parents seek out pediatricians for their kids and that as a person who wants to live in either or suburb or urban area, I'll never have the option to do hospitalists peds shifts with FM. 

So I would love some advice on that matter from people further along in their training than me

title: Manipulating your schedule/follow-ups/etc?
content:
In corporate traditional primary care, one of the few things we lowly physicians have control over is when/if our patients follow up.

Is your office jamming new est patients into your schedule? Schedule everyone for 2-3 month follow ups to blockade it.

Are you getting tons of volume that you don't want? Schedule follow ups for patients you know to be unreliable and won't show.

Cellulitis. "Better check that in 2 days" Abscess. Whatever. Come back for a "wound check." (a nice break in the schedule)...

I've never really consciously done these things, but it's entered my mind and I can see how it happens. Had an older attending at a practice once whose schedule was literally nothing but "2 month follow-up" right down the board, non-diabetics, elderly, utterly useless appointments (except maybe in the patients' non-informed minds). He protected himself well from the corporation, though I don't think did much good for the community, and I guess corporate was totally fine with this proce$$.....

EDIT: to clarify, I do NOT do this. And in fact I'm not even in corporate traditional PCP land anymore. I own a DPC and med spa. But I still think back to the hamster-wheel days...

title: First Year Attending Struggles
content:
Hey Reddit,

I hope everyone is doing well. I was hoping to post this story with a half rant and half seeking advice. I just recently graduated from residency from a rural community based family medicine program and was really proud to be a physician. It was tough work, but I got a lot of satisfaction from it. I won multiple awards while in residency, but I seem to have the personality of people either really liking me or really disliking me. I moved back to my family’s hometown afterwards though.

My first job was working at a fqhc around 15 minutes away from me. I had a lot of hope for this place but I struggled here. They did not have a good infrastructure such as a good EMR. I worked with mostly mid-levels and they honestly sucked. They had super poor care for patients and honestly had to clean up so many messes to the point of negligence. Plus, the MA’s were both rude and disrespectful to both myself and patients. I had to almost beg them to get off tiktok to room patients. I was working with a great MA, but one day a different MA yelled at me in front of patients and I just couldn’t take it any more so I crashed out and quit the job without a backup in place. Even before that, I wasn’t eating, sleeping and was putting in a lot of overtime work. In total I was there for around 2-3 months.

That brings me to my most recent job. I found it within 2 weeks of leaving my last job. It is a large hospital owned medical group with a lot more infrastructure. Mostly took HMO and PPO but it was close to my house, maybe 5 minutes away. I interviewed and within 2 weeks of leaving my past job, I found this one. The medical director seemed nice enough but she said that “we work hard, and play hard” and “we are all a family” mentality here. A little odd but ok. The other doctors here were kind and I liked them. I started to work here but it seemed that they had their cliques of medial assistants here. I was working with one who wanted to control the show based on what problems I talked about there. She works with a different doctor who is very passive, so it worked for him. However, I like my own independence and struggle with her style. When I had a complaint and brought it up with the nursing manager, she said this is “why no one wants to work with you” and was a proper dressing down. So it seems that every week they have a specific complaint about what I do in the clinic and basically have a conversation with the medical director about it. I try to be professional but it seems every mistake is set up. Just the other week, one of the Mas said something to me racial in nature so when I brought it up with the clinic manager, I was told that I should have addressed it together and that it should not have been escalated.

That brings up my medical director. I am honestly feeling like a medical resident again. She often brings me into the clinic to correct my notes saying not to write things like that or you’re typing too much. I am also having to defend my medical decision making to my medical director on a regular basis to the point where she says that I should not order labs on her patients when they come in for a physical. She says that I am practicing bad medicine and gets mad at me when I conduct USPTF guidelines for preventative care. I feel that I cannot practice independent evidence-based medicine that I am used to at my past medical residency. I brought this up before and they just say this is how she is and you are perceiving this wrong. I cannot even send referrals without her approval and on a few occasions had it denied on cases that I did not feel comfortable treating. This is more of a company wide thing though. I work more hours than the rest of the shareholder physicians as well, by at least 6 hours. They usually see around 18-19 patients a day, I see closer to 23 on a regular basis. I just started a few months ago, so I do not know how it will be with a full in-basket. They say I can join the shareholder group in 2 years though. Not sure what that entails though, but I cannot imagine surviving until then.

I hate this. I hate feeling like a resident constantly watching my step with everyone and needing to defend my medical practices to higher ups. I feel like I am walking on egg shells. This brings me to why I am writing. Some days I feel that this is a good opportunity for me to grow my practice in my hometown, but I feel genuinely unhappy. There are many different clinical settings including academic and urgent care, but not a lot of private practice. My parents want me to stay and pay my time here, but I feel that after residency, I do not want to survive, I want to thrive. Which brings me to my discussion. The job is paying around 265 plus RVU and quality bonuses which should push me up to 300k. I am debating if I should leave or if it is too soon. I feel that I will be un-hirable because I switched jobs 2 times within one year I finished residency. I may have to pay back my sign up bonus of 20k (11k after taxes), so I do not have the economic means.

\-            I stay and anticipate getting more and more burnt. It is a job which will pay the bills especially in these uncertain times. However, I do not want another crash out moment where I quit abruptly. I do not want to keep being tattled on to the point HR gets involved and my license gets put in jeopardy. The whole thing could be I am being too sensitive? 

\-            I already reached out to the higher positions to ask for a transfer and to air out my concerns. From what I understand, my clinic has been struggling to keep other doctors because I am the third doctor from 3 years that has been there and left. I am hoping to go to a different clinic to see if the culture is different elsewhere. Maybe I would go down on my hours so that I am not going for shareholder track but happy to go in and do my job. Maybe I could ask instead to do urgent care with less hours and just finish the job. However, what is the difference between leaving in 2 months vs leaving in 9 months

\-            I leave the position and do locums work in the area for a while to get my head straight. I do have feelers out there and there are plenty of positions in the area. I could start applying and interviewing for positions.

\-            Telemedicine so that I do not have to really deal with MA staff and can focus on patient care.

\-            I could try to work in the prison system. Great pay and do not mind the firearms and danger. I do not have to deal with insurance, and it seems that there is a good amount of down time. I feel that I could do this for a while I build up my DPC.

\-            Start my own dpc system. I like this option the most because it finally gives me the freedom to practice medicine I would like to do. One possibility is to start from scratch but I do not have the capital for this. Another possibility is to join with another DPC that will take 30% of my profits. This would provide overhead, supplies, and marketing for the business. That sounds a little better. However, with the new tariffs and economy, I am not sure if people would be willing to pay 75$ a month for dpc.

title: Is joining private practice or opening own practice more lucrative than hospital based group?
content:
As the title suggests. I feel that private practice just does not have enough bargaining power when it comes to getting reimbursement from insurance companies. Starting a own practice is a headache, managing overheads, employees, their schedule, medical supplies, patient panel, taxes, accounting, etc. All that with an added disadvantage of no real holidays.

Many hospital based groups offer higher RVUs or % of collection ,which can boost up salary significantly. Having said that, can joining private practice or starting own practice (traditional route, not DPC) be more lucrative? What % can you expect to earn more?

title: Have any of you left DPC to go back to an employed outpatient role? Why?
content:
Hi all! I'm about 5 years out of residency. Did my first 3 years at an FQHC, and now I'm employed by a large health system. Outpatient primary care only. I am frustrated by all of the things you would expect: pressure to see more patients than I can do a good job with, not having the freedom to close my panel even though I'm booked solid through September, inadequate support for helping my underserved patients plus employer paying me less than doctors who cherry pick easy (i.e. health literate and compliant with quality metric items) patients because I'm "less productive," annoying quality metrics BS that wastes my time clicking boxes instead of focusing on my patient, overwhelming inbox, can't retain MA because organization doesn't pay them adequately for how difficult their job is and doesn't protect them from stress, etc, etc.

So, I keep telling myself my next job will be DPC. I will not take a job like this again.

But I know I have a tendency towards "the grass is always greener" mentality. So, please tell me, those of you who left employed roles for DPC, did you ever consider going back to an employed role? Anybody who actually did go back to employed? What were your reasons?

title: How to navigate a retiring truly solo (!) primary care physician’s practice
content:
I’m looking for guidance on behalf of a my MIL who is a long-time primary care physician and sole practitioner (in every sense of the word if you see below). She is planning to retire and wants to sell her practice and possibly the office building, but she would prefer to transition it to another independent physician rather than selling to a hospital system or corporate entity. I’m a general dentist and this is very common in my world but doesn’t seem to be the case for physicians as much.

She has run this practice on her own for decades (probably since the late 80’s) and does not have any employees—she handles all her own scheduling and day to day operations. This was quite shocking to me as well!! The practice does not use electronic medical records, as she has continued with a paper-based system and not interested in converting prior to retirement. She also owns the office building (a beautiful Victorian building with another long term professional tenant) and is open to selling it along with the practice. While she currently participates with insurance, I thought the setup could be ideal for a physician looking to transition to direct primary care (DPC) and move away from the insurance model.

I’d love to hear from any physicians who have sold or purchased a similar practice—or who may know where to connect with younger doctors looking to acquire an independent office like this.

What’s the best way to find an interested buyer, particularly one who might want to convert it to a DPC model? Are there networks, forums, or organizations that focus on matching independent physicians with practices for sale? Any advice or resources would be greatly appreciated!

title: MedPeds vs Family Medicine for DPC
content:
Hello, I am only a second year medical student so forgive me for any ignorance. I have future aspirations of creating a DPC and I feel like the best specialty for it is either FM or MedPeds but I am having a hard time trying to figure out which is better. Here is my rationale in pro/ con format.

Family Medicine

Pros

\- The largest scope of all of medicine, so could craft practice to fit needs of patient population while still being in scope

\-Shorter residency by one year and easier to match into with geographic control

\- I believe most programs have more out patient procedure training which is good for DPC 

\- I believe more training in MSK, Psych, Derm, Gyn

Cons

\- Compared to MedPeds, has a fraction of Peds expertise and I feel like parents who seek out a DPC doctors have certain expectations,  and with most parents already preferring to see a pediatrician for their kid rather than an FM doctor, I feel like the lack of training in Peds would make one less marketable

\-Less competent in Peds, from what I have seen on reddit, it seems like fm doctors can handle the regular cold like symptoms, ear ache, strep throat, physicals, etc but once it becomes more than that then they refer to peds, I feel like that would defeat the purpose of a DPC

\-Can't specialize into one of the ologies so if DPC becomes unviable for some reason, stuck (would not want to do primary care if it is not through DPC)

\- Rotations in Surgery and OB, which for me is essentially wasting time in something that I will never do in any city that I would like to live in, I am also not a fan of surgery or OB 

MedPeds

Pros

\- 4 years of training dedicated to strictly adults or peds, so trades out the breadth in FM for more depth in the things that you would actually do in practice

\- Marketable: Being double certified in both Internal medicine and Pediatrics seems marketable to me, and parents that prefer their children seeing a pediatrician may appreciate that

\- More Peds knowledge: Has a higher threshold for handling complex kids without having to refer, which I think is great for DPC

\- Can further specialize incase DPC does not work out for some reason

Cons

\- Less procedure training, which would not be ideal for DPC

\- Less out patient experience in Psych, derm, gyn, etc

\- One year longer and harder to match into, and with there being less than 80 residencies in the country, very few options for desirable locations to live in

So overall I feel like there is no clear winner in terms of what would be better to match into for hopes of a dpc practice in the future, so I would love feedback from anyone who may have some insightful ideas

title: Is a better EHR system worth a pay cut?
content:
I currently work for an FQHC and am burning out hard. It’s become clear that if I want to make a career in primary care sustainable I have to make a change before I lose my mind. 

As I contemplate moving on from my current position I’ve been trying to focus on the factors related to my job that I can control. Since private practice/DPC are not options for me right now, that list is depressingly short—I’ve mostly zeroed in on the commute (I currently drive an hour each way) and choosing a new employer with a better EHR (my current clinic uses NextGen which is an absolute nightmare and adds significant time/frustration to my days).

I’m in talks with two potential employers. One uses Athena and the other is on Epic. I’ve used Epic in the past and know that I’m able to be a lot more efficient with documentation and inbasket management. I’ve never used Athena. However, pay and benefits are much better with the clinic that uses Athena—it would be a step up in compensation, while the system that uses Epic would actually be a pay cut of around $10k annually compared to my current salary. 

Obviously I’m not keen on taking a pay cut, but my primary goal right now is to improve my quality of life and do less work at home. I’m just so sick of coming home frustrated by dysfunctional clinic dynamics and then still having hours of charting to do before bed. 

Is being on a more functional EHR worth a lower salary if it makes your life easier? Would also really appreciate hearing perspectives on using Athena and if folks find it efficient compared with Epic.

title: Anyone worried about media shifting blame for healthcare costs to physicians in the wake of UHC CEO public outrage?
content:
Starting to see more and more takes that physicians are the “real” problem with health care costs. This is worrisome because it not only puts even more of a target on physician’s backs making my job more unsafe (I still have my name up on our residency website & I’m sure some internet sleuth could probably deduce where I live too. Meanwhile CEOs are taking their names offline). 

The other worry is that on both sides, I’m afraid there will be a targeted effort to slash physician salaries & reimbursements even further. And as a young physician with exorbitant student loans to pay off, I’ve broken down my post-residency budget, and with my loan pay offs factored in, I will still be straddled with a lot of debt. (Housing prices are also ridiculous). Yea, I’m in a “more privileged” position but I am nowhere near swimming in CEO money, and CEOs don’t have med school debt lol. 

I just can see the public jumping on this bandwagon (just read an article about a patient who was mad that her “physician billed her” for an office procedure, but no anger for the fact that her insurance company decided not to cover that procedure 🫠). 

Unfortunately I do a lot of catastrophizing (yeah, I should probably be on an SSRI lol) but is the solution, specifically for FM, to just pivot towards DPC/cash-pay only if the tide turns against us? 

Doesn’t seem like physicians will be unionizing in any meaningful way soon. We’re in this weird privileged but also hostage situation where we are part of the “elite” in that we are doctors but we are also still cogs in the wheel because there’s so many industry factors and barriers that we have no control over, but we have to find a way to still make a way that allows us to break even on the investment we made with our time & education & training.

Sometimes when I see the hit pieces on doctors I feel resentful, and I just want to go on some kind of strike. But we would be spun as the bad guys there too if we “let patients die”

Any sobering takes on this to talk me down? Anyone have plan b options their considering if/when/as our healthcare infrastructure falls apart?

title: Subreddit State of the Union 2024
content:
# Another year, another annual mod update!

Thank you everyone for all the contributions and growth of this community over the past year - we've almost doubled in size, and it's been really great to see how the subreddit has changed over the years. Below is a summary of the most recent developments, works in process and hopes for upcoming projects. And as always, we welcome feedback from you all about what you want to see/don't want to see for the subreddit.

**- mandatory user flair:** added earlier this year to distinctly display a person's job status (MD/DO/resident/RN/layperson etc) and has cut significantly down on spam and non-medical persons posting! If you have a specific request for user flair not currently listed, message mods.

**- optional verified user flair:** want to show your flair as verified? [Click here](https://www.reddit.com/r/FamilyMedicine/wiki/index/) to read how to apply for verified user flair in the Wiki. Also can [click here](https://www.reddit.com/r/FamilyMedicine/comments/18rqxgq/important_mod_update_user_flair/) for a post with FAQ about user flair.

**- expanded wiki resource:** on the right sidebar, the wiki contains info about the subreddit moderation standards, applicant resources, residency topics including exams, and a career tab that is in process but currently includes a FAQ about DPC practice.

**- trimonthly jobs & career thread:** had heard multiple times that the # of career posts was getting a bit excessive on the main page, everyone voted to have a stickied thread to collate the posts while also leaving career posts on the main page. So we now have 2 stickied posts (which is our maximum), one for students and one for job posts. It's not used very frequently, I have some hope that this will catch on but honestly it doesn't seem to be, is usually empty, and will likely be phased out some point over the next several months if it doesn't pick up steam. (There are other things I'd like to have in a stickied post, things much more exciting, as below).

**- what is continuing to be worked on/ideas for future:** expanding career resources and info, start some sort of advocacy in FM resource, establish a schedule of AMA's on variety of topics (different practice models, AMA with recruiter, FM/OB AMA, rural practice AMA, etc). Goal for the year is set up a recurring AMA event. If you're interested in doing an AMA, message mods!! Would love to hear if there is interest.

Cheers to the next year, and thank you to everyone who finds any source of community here, whether by posts, comments, or just stalking the page as a silent participant and reader.

title: Long term viability of DPC?
content:
Hi, I’m a first year med student and I am very interested in FM and potentially starting a DPC practice one day. I love the autonomy and the flexibility that DPC seems to offer. I’ve shadowed a DPC doc and she seems to really love her work. 

I realize that I can certainly change my mind about this since I’ve got a hell of a long way to go still but honestly as silly as it sounds I find myself daydreaming about what my practice will look like, be named, etc.

Anyways given that I’ve got at least seven years until I’m in any position close to opening a practice, are there any looming threats to DPCs to just keep in the back of one’s mind? It seems like the community of DPC doctors is very passionate and active but of course there could be challenges to the practice model by bad players in the government and/or private health insurance that make the practice model less viable. 

Another concern I had was that the market for DPC might be saturated within the next 10 years. Practices are popping up like crazy it seems and I wonder if there will be a point where every who wants and can afford to join a DPC already has. 

Again, I’m a lowly M1 and know nothing. Would appreciate anyone’s thoughts on this!

title: Direct primary care revenue model for preventive services
content: For those of you with direct primary care practices, what is your revenue model for offering routine screening services? When it comes to ordering tests to investigate symptoms or to monitor chronic health conditions, then it seems reasonable to set expectations that patients will have to cover whatever fees are charged by your lab contractor (e.g. LabCorp), but what about when it comes to things like routine cholesterol screening? Do you include preventive testing in your membership fee, or are those costs individually passed onto your patients, too? In the latter scenario, it seems like DPC for uninsured patients would be particularly costly to women, as I imagine paying cash for Pap smears and mammograms is not cheap.

title: "Micro practice" model? Why isn't it done more?
content:
Hey all - incoming MS1 interested in primary care. Everywhere I turn (as a pt myself), insurance is the enemy.

Any stories/information people have on people successfully cutting out the middleman in a NON-concierge style practice (including non-DPC.. which is interesting, but asking for a FFS model without insurance).

For example, the FM doc that set up a [$35/visit (now at $40)](https://www.wtae.com/article/pittsburgh-doctor-timothy-wong-35-dollars-with-without-insurance/30969261) urgent-care type microclinic. Just him & an iPad. He charges extra for more complex visits, but not by much. Looks like he's still open after 4 years since the article was written.

Essentially the model is stay as lean as possible & do not bill insurance (which helps you stay lean). In the above example, he doesn't even have reception, pts just check in on an iPad.

So a buddy of mine went to an urgent care (uninsured) for an STD & after a physical exam referred him to the ER for 200$. My deductible to see my PCM was $120 last visit. Why isn't this model just blatantly out competing an urgent care? Rent an office space & see patients for cheaper than urgent care/deductible.

The math is @ 40$/visit, open 5 days a week, closed 2 weeks out of the year (W=50)

= 40 \* 5 \* 50 \* (Patients Seen) = $200,000 (20 pt per day)

Your overhead is rent (tiny office), utilities, EMR, and malpractice insurance (am I missing anything else?),

Let's say overhead is 40k/year & you take home $160,000.

I see that you are **WAY** under what newly employed FM physician makes. But- Set your own schedule, earn what you do- Minimize the "running your own business" since you are almost not hiring at all.- Less documentation since you aren't documenting for insurance/coding- Less documentation/coding in general- Not accepting insurance means less government regulation (no medicare/medicaid)- You are not at the whim of insurance companies (contracts, new regulations, recent Change Healthcare hack), so you are truly independent

Is it just about the $/economics?

​

Edit: Here are two interviews with a doc that is doing this model:

1. [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jJl2uWTJhJs&t=8s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jJl2uWTJhJs&t=8s)
2. [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E6qo2HgED7M](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E6qo2HgED7M)
3. [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sCb\_MlNhmEo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sCb_MlNhmEo)

Summary: volume 15-32 pt per day ($35 for most visits), only provider, iPad, etc. 700 sqft office space, if you are interested about how someone is pulling this off!

title: Am I being naive going into FM?
content:
Soon to be M4 here who is heavily considering applying FM this year. My main reasons are:

1. I want to be a generalist. I get bored in specialty rotations seeing the same organ system/things over and over again, so that kind of narrows it down to FM/EM/IM. Out of those 3 I prefer the clinic over the hospital.
2. I like the versatility of what you can do and where you can practice: outpatient clinic/hospitalist/urgent care/DPC/rural ER etc.
3. Work-life balance. I really, really would like to work a 4-day workweek once I'm an attending, and part-time once I'm older, and I've heard FM is one of the main specialties in medicine where this is doable.

However, I hear a lot of conflicting things about FM lifestyle. There are the stories of people seeing 30-40 patients a day and being buried in admin work and paperwork for most of their off-time, which legitimately sounds like a nightmare to me and I'd rather go back to being a scribe than do that. I've also read stories of people saying they see 18 patients a day for 30 mins at a time, 4 days a week, which definitely sounds more desirable and doable to me.

Am I being naive by thinking by doing FM it will be easy and doable to find reasonably paced 4-day workweek jobs out there?  Or is the job market generally bleaker than that in terms of workload? Money is not a big driver for me and I would be happy making $150k a year if I had a chill work-life balance.

title: Addiction Med Q&A
content:
I have had a good number of people reach out to me expressing interest and asking questions about Addiction Medicine.  Bear in mind that I'm just a PGY-5 FM MD in the mid-west.  One of the best things about AdMed IMO is that any specialty can put it into practice and the variability even within a specialty can be dramatic.  Would love to hear other addiction docs' input and feedback, so please feel free to have at it.

Apologies for the length and redundancy, but I just don't have the time or energy to post a polished long-form product right now.  My plan is to come back to this and continue to edit/add to it.  Will do my best to answer other questions in comments too.

Cheers!

P.S. u/darthbeeman wrote up [a fantastic post detailing his journey](https://www.reddit.com/r/AddictionMedicine/comments/1497rwf/addiction_medicine_practice_pathway_education_and/) through the process as well. Highly recommend checking that out for more reading.

——————————————————————————————

**User1**

Hey! What is Job outlook like now addiction Med? Any info on salary numbers?

**abertheham**

Job outlook is open to whatever you want to do with it, i.e. it depends on what proportion of your time and practice you want to commit to it. I work mostly in primary care and take internal referrals from colleagues to provide outpatient treatment and/or evals to funnel patients into higher levels of care. But some people choose to work exclusively in addiction, in settings like inpatient treatment facilities, hospital consultation services, detox centers, and OTPs. The field is still new so the possibilities are largely open to your imagination and networking opportunities.

Salary is going to be dependent on which of those contexts you choose to work in, but is largely based on your primary board certification.

**User1**

Do you have any advice on what to do to improve CV if looking to go into addiction Med?

**abertheham**

Depends on the program, but most of them are not super competitive. The past few years there haven't been enough applicants to fill all the fellowships, so it's not like you need to really impress on paper. I'd say a good personal statement will take you a lot further. Being genuine in your desire to care for people and improve your knowledge base will go a long ways.

It wouldn't hurt to have publications, QI projects, volunteering experience that shows some predilection toward working with use disorders, but I wouldn't say that's critical.

As I interviewed potential fellows last year, it felt like some applicants were doing addiction medicine and/or applying to our program just because it showed up in their list on ERAS. Programs are obviously going to want to know why you want to train with them specifically, so do your best to make that come through as well.

Sorry if that's not quite the answer you were looking for--happy to clarify or answer other questions

**User1**

Thank you so much!

What does it mean that people applied to your program just because you showed up on eras?

If geography is preference would that not show? Or I guess would have to show that in the personal statement?

In terms of competitiveness, I’ll be applying when they close the pathway so the only way to get certified is through fellowship. You don’t think it will get more competitive then?

**abertheham**

I just meant it seemed like they threw out applications because our program was in a list of available programs—had no prior ties or interest in the region, didn’t seem to know much about the program at all or really have any interest in the area or anything you know? Not necessarily a bad thing in itself but it’s just not a great look when you don’t have an answer to “what drew you to/motivated you to apply to this program”

Hard to say what will happen to the competitiveness. Where are you at in your training?

As it stands right now, the salary is mostly influenced by primary board certification and there’s still a lot of stigma around the field, so I don’t see it getting dramatically more competitive in the next 3-5 years

**User1**

Ah okay I see. How do you find out more about programs if they don’t have much listed on their site? I tried finding any fellowship residency fairs but was not successful in that.

Just started pgy2

And I am in FM now

Oh okay awesome! Thanks!

**abertheham**

That’s a good question and a fair point actually. I guess maybe calling or emailing to ask for details would be the best avenue if there’s not much online. Otherwise just showing curiosity and asking for those details during the interview while also showing interest in AdMed as a whole and/or the geographic region.

I think maybe what I was getting at was that we interviewed a couple who seemed strangely ambivalent about the whole endeavor and that just wasn’t a good look.

And congrats on getting through intern year. I always tell people, that was the real, actual turning point where it finally stopped getting progressively shittier in training. Always thought getting through MCAT and into med school would be the hard part, then it just got worse and harder until after intern year, it FINALLY started easing up a little. Different kinds stressors still existed for me no doubt but on the whole, it felt like that’s when things actually turned around for the better. I lost that “it’s bad now but it’s gonna get worse” mindset. Idk how your program is, but hopefully the rest of residency is good to you. It does eventually end so hang in there.

**User1**

Okay thank you! I see what you mean!

Thank you so much!! I really appreciate it!!

**abertheham** 

Any time!

——————————————————————————————

**User2**

Hello! Saw your comment about addiction med, thanks for being open for some questions! I basically thought only after 2025 admed will require fellowship…right now i thought you only needed to take the test ? what’s the most exciting part of your day when directly related to admed? thanks so much

**abertheham**

Hey! Sure, it's my pleasure. I can't remember the exact dates of when things will change, but the short version is that the people who grandfathered into the training via non-fellowship routes can continue, but basically the only way to start down the path now is through a fellowship. I think. That was the only path that was relevant to me, so I don't know the ins and outs of the practice pathway route or anything like that. I'm like 99% sure you can't just sit for the board exam anymore though.

The most exciting part of my day is meeting people where they're at. Ad med gets a lot of eye-rolls and 'oh man I bet that's a difficult population' kind of reactions, but it's an incredibly fulfilling field. What a lot of people don't consider is that by the time someone with a use disorder is sitting in your specialty clinic, they really just want help. I really enjoy employing harm reduction techniques and the open discourse that can genuinely give people their lives back in an incredibly powerful way. Suboxone is an incredible medication and I just love getting people with OUD started on it.

It definitely comes with its own set of unique challenges, and some cases ultimately prove tragic/fatal, but yeah... high highs and low lows, ya know?

Its also nice to be the one people turn to when they don't know how to handle those tricky situations. The education part and working to end stigma is quite important as well--both with patients and colleagues.

And finally, I guess I'd say that I like walking around with the knowledge that I could ditch primary care and go do specialty work in pretty much any setting, and finding that job (or building it from scratch) will be a lot easier with the dual board certification.

**User2**

Wow these are all amazing considerations and insights. Thank you so much for your reply and may you continue to have the positive impact on the people’s live you touch, you are appreciated!

——————————————————————————————

**User3**

Hello! I saw a comment on reddit of yours about chill medical specialties and im looking into addiction med but I wanted to ask your thoughts about lifestyle and compensation?

**abertheham**

Hey, sorry I just got this and am about to go to bed but am happy to discuss whenever.

The “short” version is lifestyle can be what you make it, but it does depend on your primary specialty to some extent. Compensation tends to be more or less the same as your primary specialty - possibly less if it was a high-dollar specialty, or possibly slightly more if it’s an adjunctive part of your practice.

It’s still a relatively new field so there is not like a single “typical” pathway or work scenario. That flexibility affords a lot of possibilities for great work/life balance. Anything from research and clinical trials, to primary care, to methadone clinics and residential treatment facilities; pain clinics, palliative clinics… it kind of runs the gambit.

Compensation will pretty much always be adequate as a physician in the US, imo, but then I live fairly modestly (not \*that\* modestly though) and went into family practice, so my perspective is likely to be quite different than some of the super competitive subspecialties that aim to take it from 6 figures to 7…

**User3**

You’re all good! I would love to optimize compensation and the variety of practice setting now! I’m between addiction and sleep and leaning more towards addiction rn but what do you think? What type of practice setting do you do now?

**abertheham**

I’m obviously biased towards addiction, but sleep is interesting too.

I’m about to start my first big boy job in a primary clinic doing mostly FM but taking referrals for addiction treatment. Depending on demand that may expand to have dedicated addiction days, e-consults, or an addiction-only practice.

I enjoy FM and want to practice it initially at least, but I’m open to being drawn into a sub specialty if the work shows up (or if primary care goes all the way to shit).

**User3**

Hi! I realized we ve talked before! I do really want to practice addiction and grow full time eventually and I hope I’m able to build a good private practice model and I was wondering how job variety is and compensation is?

**abertheham**

Variety is great—you can do pretty much whatever you like with it. Some run outpatient addiction clinics, some do inpatient rehab/detox management, some do hospital consult/liaison, some run methadone clinics… Demand is high so you can sort of choose your own adventure so-to-speak.

Compensation is variable because it’s going to be heavily based on your primary board certification.

**User3**

I’d love to do a variety with outpatient and inpatient consults with managing rehab/detox centers!

But my primary certification is FM!

**abertheham**

That’s perfect, tbh.

**User3**

My parents are Asian and I apologize for asking about compensation. They made me feel bad about choosing FM and choosing addiction because they don’t think I’ll be able to live a comfortable nice life with addiction

I apologize and thank you for your input

**abertheham** 

Bit harder for peds or IM because addiction knows no boundaries. With an FM primary, you can manage addiction in everyone from pregnancy/neonatal through geriatrics.

**User3**

So I wanted to be able to scale and build a private practice

**abertheham**

Hah no worries. It’s definitely a real consideration. Are you still in residency?

**User3**

I am! I’m a 3rd year now! I’ve been on night float teaching the new interns

I’ve been working through my application and my addiction personal statement in the midst of all of it

**abertheham**

Regardless, I’m not sure how much you’ve looked into the job market, but FM compensation isn’t anything to bat an eye at…

You can work 4 days a week in a city making 250k+ or work your ass off and make a half million going rural, doing DPC, or something. Either way, life is comfortable.

**User3**

That’s good to hear! Personally though, especially after nights and flipping back and forth, I mainly want to prioritize my long term health and happiness

title: How certain were you about family medicine before you began medical school?

title: USMD student at a great school interested in FM, but ONLY if it's DPC.. is FM worth it?
content:
I'm only an M1 so please forgive me for any mistakes in reasoning, but long story short I'm super interested in family medicine but I don't think I could see myself practicing traditionally. 

Seeing 20+ patients a day, spending hours dealing with insurance and charting, while having compensation that doesn't reflect the work that has to be put in. 

I just don't see how that can be sustainable and if I was forced to practice like that I would rather not and I'd consider a specialty that would be the next best thing. 

The thing is I really like the idea of fm, I love the idea of being someone's doctor, forming long term relationships with my patients who trust me with their life, being a generalist and knowing enough to handle the concerns of most of the issues most patients would ever have. 

I feel like having a DPC practice would essentially eliminate those problems I listed earlier thus providing what for me would be the best gig in medicine. ( ik it comes with its own cons like dealing with running a business but I'd MUCH rather have that problem than the alternative). 

So my question is, does it make sense to pursue fm knowing that I would only be happy having my own DPC practice? Or is it too risky being that some legislation could be passed to make it impractical, would love to hear any thoughts
